n: The Lord sends the prophet Nathan to confront David. Wisely, Nathan doesn’t accuse him directly but tells a story, as if presenting a legal case for the king to judge.

f.g: The parable lets David judge the situation honestly before realizing it is about himself.

n: The rich man has huge flocks and herds — more than he could ever need.
The poor man has just one little lamb that he loves like a daughter. The tender details — eating from his plate, sleeping in his arms — make the injustice deeply personal.

f.g: Slept in his arms — a picture of love and closeness, echoing how a wife is cherished.

n: When a guest arrives, the rich man refuses to use his own animals and instead takes and cooks the poor man’s only lamb.
David is furious and swears the man deserves to die. Without realizing it, he has pronounced judgment on himself.

f.g: Literally “is a son of death” — deserves death.

n: David also rules that the man must repay four lambs, as the law required. Tradition notes that four of David’s sons later suffered or died.
Nathan’s four Hebrew words cut to the heart: “You are the man.” Then he speaks for the Lord, recounting all God had done for David.

f.g: In Hebrew just two words: ’attah ha’ish.

n: God had given David everything — Saul’s kingdom and household, all Israel and Judah — and would have given more if he had asked.

f.g: The harem of a former king passed to his successor as a sign of royal authority.

n: God names the sins plainly: David despised the Lord’s commandment, murdered Uriah using the enemy’s sword, and took his wife.

f.w: despised the commandment of the LORD

n: The consequence: violence will never leave David’s household. In the coming chapters three of his sons — Amnon, Absalom, and Adonijah — die violently.

f.w: the sword shall never depart from thine house

n: Trouble will rise from within David’s own family, and his wives will be taken publicly by another — fulfilled when Absalom rebels.

f.w: lie with thy wives in the sight of this sun

n: David sinned in secret, but his punishment will be public. What is done in darkness is brought into the light.

David doesn’t make excuses; he confesses simply, “I have sinned against the Lord.” Nathan says David will not die, as the law required for adultery and murder. Latter-day Saint scripture teaches that David’s sin against Uriah still cost him eternal blessings.

f.w: I have sinned against the LORD

n: Because David’s sin gave God’s enemies a reason to mock the Lord and His people, the child will die. Our sins can harm the reputation of God’s work.

f.w: given great occasion to the enemies of the LORD to blaspheme

n: Nathan leaves, and the baby becomes seriously ill. Note that the child’s mother is called “Uriah’s wife,” a reminder of the wrong done.
David pleads with God for the child, fasting and lying on the ground all night in sackcloth-like humility.
His senior servants try to lift him up and get him to eat, but he refuses.
On the seventh day the child dies. The servants are afraid to tell David, fearing what he might do in his grief.

f.g: Do himself harm; be overwhelmed with distress.

n: David notices them whispering and realizes the child is gone.
To everyone’s surprise, David gets up, washes, changes clothes, worships at the Lord’s house, and then eats. He accepts God’s will and turns to Him in worship even in sorrow.

f.g: Put on oil — a sign of ending mourning (compare 2 Samuel 14:2).
The tent sanctuary where the ark was kept; the temple was not yet built.

n: His servants are confused: he mourned while the child lived, but stopped once it died.
David explains that while the child lived, there was hope that God might be gracious.
Now nothing can bring the child back — but David expresses hope that he will go to his son one day. Latter-day Saints teach that little children who die are saved through Christ’s Atonement.

f.w: I shall go to him, but he shall not return to me

n: David comforts Bath-sheba, and she bears another son, Solomon. The narrator adds a tender note of grace: the Lord loved him.
Through Nathan, the Lord gives the baby a second name, Jedidiah, “beloved of the LORD.” The same prophet who brought judgment now brings a sign of God’s continuing favor.

f.g: “Beloved of Jehovah”; it shares a root with David’s name, which also suggests “beloved.”

n: The story returns to the war that framed David’s sin. Joab captures the part of Rabbah that holds the royal quarter.

f.g: Perhaps the citadel or the part of the city containing the palace.

n: Joab reports that he has taken the “city of waters” — the city’s water supply — so the rest of the city cannot hold out long.

f.g: Likely the lower city or fortification protecting the water source.

n: Joab urges David to come and finish the conquest himself, so the victory will be credited to the king — perhaps a pointed reminder that David belongs with his army.
David finally goes to battle and takes Rabbah.
David takes the crown of the Ammonite king (or of their god Milcom), a massive gold crown weighing about a talent, and much plunder.

f.g: The Hebrew malkam can mean “their king” or Milcom, the Ammonite god (1 Kings 11:5).
A talent weighed roughly 75 pounds (34 kg) — too heavy to wear long, so perhaps worn only briefly or on ceremonial occasions.

n: The Ammonite people are put to work with saws, picks, and axes and in brickmaking. Many translators read this as forced labor rather than torture. Then David and the army return to Jerusalem.

f.g: The Hebrew can mean he set them to work with saws — forced labor.
Possibly the brick mold — making bricks as forced labor.
